headline: Canarsie Pier at First Light: Fluke in the Channel, Blues in the Shallows
subhead: The bay's split into two shifts right now — daytime fish in the deep water, bass waiting for dark, and the weakfish starting to show like we thought they would.
body_markdown:
I launched the kayak off Canarsie Pier before six this morning, and I picked that spot on purpose. With the bay running warm through the afternoons, the early paddle out to the edge of the flats is the only window where you're not fighting the sun and the heat both. Canarsie gives me quick access to the channel edge without a long haul, and it lets me check three different things in one trip — the deep water for fluke, the shallows for snapper blues, and the general mood of the bay before it gets crowded.

Fluke are the most dependable thing going right now, and they're doing exactly what they do in the heat — sitting deep, off the mud and sand transitions in Grassy Bay and along the channel edges by the Cross Bay Bridge, and feeding hardest on the moving water. I've been dragging four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter- and half-ounce bucktails, slow enough that I can feel the bottom the whole drift, and the fish have been there on both the incoming and outgoing — just tucked a little deeper than they were in June. Fifteen to twenty feet has been the sweet spot. Nothing enormous, but a steady pick of keepers mixed with plenty of shorts, which is honestly what July fluking in the bay looks like most years. If you want a shot at a bigger fish, work the deeper holes off Motts Basin on the last two hours of the ebb, when the bait gets funneled out with the current.

Snapper blues are thick in every shallow corner of the bay right now — off the pier, along the bulkheads, up in the coves by Bergen Basin. This is the easiest, most reliable action going, and it's exactly the stuff that gets a kid hooked on fishing for life. Small hooks, a strip of spearing or a sliver of bunker under a bobber, and you'll have a bucket of them in twenty minutes. Nothing fancy needed.

The striped bass have gone nocturnal, and that's not them disappearing — it's a heat response. Daytime bay temps have been sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, and that pushes the bass off the flats and into deeper structure until the sun goes down. Marine Parkway Bridge is still the number-one spot, but you need to fish it after dark now to get consistent results. I've had my best luck working the outgoing tide, casting bucktails and swimming plugs tight to the pilings and current breaks under the bridge lights, letting the sweep carry the lure through the seam. The bite window tends to open an hour or two after sunset and hold through the strongest push of the outgoing water. Daytime trips around the bridge have been mostly quiet — don't waste your morning there right now.

We flagged this last week — said the weakfish bite would start rebuilding on calm, warm evenings as the bay settled into summer — and that's exactly what's starting to happen. I had two solid weakfish in the four-pound class off Ruffle Bar on a still evening, working a chartreuse soft plastic on a light jighead just as the light was fading and the water went glassy. It's not a full-blown bite yet, more like the first real signs of one, but if you can get out on a calm evening around the marsh edges — Ruffle Bar, the flats off Grassy Bay, the deeper holes near the Raunt — that's where I'd put my money over the next couple weeks.

Bluefish have been the story everywhere south and west of us — bunker schools stacking up along the Jersey beaches and pushing north, and it's worth keeping an eye on Rockaway Beach because that pattern has a habit of sliding up the coast as the bait moves with it. Nothing's blown up on the Rockaway sand yet, but if the bunker show, the blues won't be far behind, and that's a fast, violent bite when it turns on — bucktails, poppers, whatever you've got, just be ready to move fast.

Porgies are still worth a stop if you're fishing the rocks around Rockaway Inlet — small hooks, bloodworms or clam, and you can put together a nice mess of them on the bottom stages of the tide.

With the moon heading toward first quarter on the 21st, the current's easing up a bit, which usually means slower, more deliberate presentations pay off better than a fast retrieve — that's especially true for the fluke and the weakfish. Looking ahead, if the calm, stable weather holds, I'd expect the weakfish pattern to keep building on quiet evenings, the bass to stay locked into their after-dark rhythm around the bridge until the nights cool off some, and fluke to remain the most consistent daytime bet in the deeper channels. If the bunker push north and Rockaway Beach lights up with bluefish, I'll be out there — but for now, my time's split between a dawn paddle for fluke and a dusk cast for weakfish, and that's not a bad way to spend a July week on this bay.
